title: Don't @ in DMs. — they already get the notification
metaDescription: A 40-scenario quiz on @mentioning people in Slack DMs. In a 1:1 DM, every message and every thread reply already notifies them, even in a thread they haven't joined. Drop the @.
thesis: Starting a DM with @Sam feels like making sure Sam sees it. Sam was always going to see it. In a direct message, the message is the ping, and that includes every thread reply, even in a thread Sam hasn't touched yet.

explainer.body: By default, Slack notifies you when someone sends you a direct message. Threads too: "By default, you'll be notified of new replies to all threads in one-to-one DMs." (Slack: Use threads) All threads means all of them, including one you just started under your own message that they haven't replied in yet. In a two-person DM, they don't need to join a thread to hear from it. Adding an @ doesn't make that notification any louder.

"In channels or DMs with multiple people, you'll be notified of new replies if you started the thread, replied to it, or were mentioned." (Slack: Use threads) So if someone in a group DM hasn't touched the thread, the @ is the only thing that reaches them.

trap: The trap: The @ feels like insurance. In a 1:1 DM it insures against nothing, because they were getting that notification anyway. What it actually adds is tone: @Sam at the top of a private message reads like tapping on the glass. It also won't get past paused notifications. For a real emergency, Slack gives DM senders a once-a-day "notify anyway" override, and that's a separate button, not an @.
quizHeading: Quiz: does this message need the @?

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM with Sam, you write: "@Sam do you have 10 minutes this afternoon?"

why.plain: Right. It's a DM, so Sam gets notified the moment you hit send. "Do you have 10 minutes?" says everything.
why.at: Redundant ping. The DM already notifies Sam, so the @ adds nothing except a faint whiff of impatience.

scenarios.q: Sam asked a question in a thread in your 1:1 DM, and you reply in that thread: "@Sam yep, ship it."

why.plain: Right. Slack notifies both people of every thread reply in a 1:1 DM by default. "Yep, ship it" lands.
why.at: This is the myth the site exists for. Threads in 1:1 DMs notify on every reply, so the @ is decoration.

scenarios.q: You're replying in a thread in your 1:1 DM with your manager, under a message they sent last week.

why.plain: Right. Even an old thread notifies on new replies in a 1:1 DM. Age doesn't matter.
why.at: Belt-and-suspenders ping. Old or new, a 1:1 DM thread reply already reaches them.

scenarios.q: In a group DM with Lee and Priya, a thread exists between you and Lee, and now you need Priya, who hasn't said a word in it, to confirm the budget.

why.plain: Silent miss. In a group DM, thread replies only notify people who started the thread, replied, or were mentioned. Priya is none of those.
why.at: Right. This is the legit case: a group-DM thread where the person hasn't joined in. Without the @, Priya never sees it.

scenarios.q: Jordan said "ping me when the build is green" in your 1:1 DM, and now it's green.

why.plain: Right. "Build's green" in the DM is the ping. That's what a DM is.
why.at: Double tap. Jordan asked for a ping, and a DM already is one. Spelling it "@Jordan" doesn't make it more of one.

scenarios.q: Your teammate has paused notifications, and you want an @ in your DM to break through because it's urgent.

why.plain: Right. An @ doesn't pierce paused notifications. For a genuine emergency, Slack offers DM senders a once-a-day "notify anyway" override, so use that or just call them.
why.at: Wrong tool. Paused is paused, and an @ won't get through. The DM override is a separate, deliberate button.

scenarios.q: You open a fresh DM to a new hire on day one: "@Riley welcome aboard! Holler if you need anything."

why.plain: Right. "Welcome aboard, Riley!" is warmer anyway, and the DM notifies them regardless.
why.at: It's a welcome note, not a page. The @ makes a friendly message read like a ticket assignment.

scenarios.q: In a five-person group DM, a thread is going between you and Ana, and you need Ben, who hasn't replied, to check a number.

why.plain: Silent miss. Ben isn't following the thread, so a plain reply won't notify him.
why.at: Right. In a group-DM thread, the @ is how a non-participant hears about it, and the mention also subscribes him to future replies.

scenarios.q: Lee started a thread in your group DM, and you're replying to answer Lee's question.

why.plain: Right. Lee started the thread, so Lee gets notified of replies. No @ needed.
why.at: Redundant. Starting the thread already subscribed Lee. The @ is a second knock on an open door.

scenarios.q: Priya already replied in a group-DM thread an hour ago, and now you're answering her follow-up.

why.plain: Right. Replying subscribed Priya to the thread, so she'll get yours.
why.at: Redundant. Once someone's replied in a thread, they're following it. The @ adds noise, not reach.

scenarios.q: Someone in your group-DM thread was @mentioned earlier in it, and you're now replying to what they said.

why.plain: Right. Being mentioned earlier is one of the three ways into a thread's notifications. They're already in.
why.at: Re-mentioning someone who's already following just stacks pings. One mention per thread is enough.

scenarios.q: You send your weekly status update to your manager in your 1:1 DM, opening with "@Morgan, weekly update:".

why.plain: Right. "Weekly update:" is the whole header. It's a DM, so Morgan gets notified.
why.at: Ceremony, not signal. The @ on a recurring DM update trains Morgan to tune out your mentions.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you send three messages in a row, and each one starts with "@Kim".

why.plain: Right. Every one of those messages already notifies Kim. Better still, fold them into one message.
why.at: Three @s in a private conversation reads like someone banging on the door.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you share a link: "@Alex saw this and thought of you."

why.plain: Right. "Saw this and thought of you" lands fine without the @. It's a DM.
why.at: A friendly share with an @ attached reads more like an assignment than a gift.

scenarios.q: In a 1:1 DM, you tell Sam: "ask @Priya, she owns billing". Priya isn't in the DM.

why.plain: "Ask Priya" leaves Sam guessing which Priya and how to find her. A non-pinging profile link is pure help.
why.at: Right. Per Slack, people who aren't in the DM aren't notified, so here the @ is just a clickable name tag for Sam.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, Sam hasn't answered for an hour, so you follow up with "@Sam bump".

why.plain: Right. A follow-up DM notifies them again on its own. If an hour of silence matters, say why: "need this by 3 for the client call."
why.at: Escalating with an @ in a DM changes nothing mechanically and plenty tonally. It reads as "I am watching you not reply."

scenarios.q: You're schedule-sending a DM to a coworker for Monday 9am, and you add an @ so they don't miss it.

why.plain: Right. A scheduled DM is still a DM when it lands, so it notifies like any other.
why.at: Scheduling doesn't weaken the notification, so the @ is still insurance against nothing.

scenarios.q: In a group DM with Dana and Eli, Dana opened a thread with you, and now you need Eli, who hasn't seen it, to make the call.

why.plain: Silent miss. Eli didn't start the thread, didn't reply, and wasn't mentioned, so Eli gets nothing.
why.at: Right. Group-DM thread plus a non-participant you need is exactly the case the @ was built for.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you reply in-thread to their message from this morning: "@Taylor done, merged."

why.plain: Right. 1:1 DM threads notify both people on every reply by default.
why.at: Redundant. The thread you're in is in a two-person DM, and both of you get every reply.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM with a partner via Slack Connect, you open with "@Jamie quick question on the contract."

why.plain: Right. A DM is a DM, even across companies. "Quick question on the contract" is plenty.
why.at: Same redundancy with an outside partner, and a little brusque when you're representing your company.

scenarios.q: In a four-person group DM, you post a new top-level message and need one specific person to own the decision.

why.plain: Everyone's notified, but with no name nobody knows it's theirs, and the decision stalls in a three-way game of chicken.
why.at: Right, with a caveat: the @ isn't for the notification (everyone got that). It's assigning ownership in a room of four.

scenarios.q: In a group DM, you post meeting notes top-level for everyone, with each person @mentioned in the first line.

why.plain: Right. Top-level messages in a DM notify everyone in it. Save @s for the line where a specific person owns an action.
why.at: A roll call of @s on a message everyone already gets is just volume.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you remind a coworker: "@Chris reminder, the deck is due Friday."

why.plain: Right. "Reminder: deck's due Friday" in a DM notifies Chris on its own.
why.at: Adding an @ to a reminder makes it read like an escalation. The DM was already the nudge.

scenarios.q: Your coworker is on vacation, and you @ them in the DM so it's "top of their list" when they're back.

why.plain: Right. It'll sit as an unread DM when they return either way. If it's truly first priority, say so in words.
why.at: No priority boost. A DM is already unread and badged, and the @ doesn't jump the queue.

scenarios.q: You started a thread in your group DM, and Max replied, so now you're answering Max.

why.plain: Right. Max replied, so Max is following the thread and will get yours.
why.at: Redundant. Max subscribed themselves the moment they replied.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you send a doc for review: "@Pat could you look at this by EOD?"

why.plain: Right. "Could you look at this by EOD?" with the link is the whole message, and the DM notifies Pat.
why.at: The deadline does the work, and the @ just adds pressure on top of it.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM thread, Sam replied 30 seconds ago and you write back "@Sam yep."

why.plain: Right. You're mid-conversation in a two-person thread. "Yep" lands instantly.
why.at: Live back-and-forth plus an @ is like saying someone's name in every sentence across a small table.

scenarios.q: In a group DM, you need someone who hasn't touched a thread to take over the task being discussed in it.

why.plain: Silent miss. They're not subscribed to the thread, so the handoff never reaches them and the task stalls.
why.at: Right. The @ notifies them and subscribes them to the thread, so the handoff actually lands.

scenarios.q: In a group DM, you post a top-level "we shipped it!" to the three people who worked on it.

why.plain: Right. Everyone in a group DM gets top-level messages. Celebrate without the roll call.
why.at: Three @s on a celebration nobody could miss is just volume.

scenarios.q: You worry your 1:1 DM won't show up in their Activity tab, so you add an @.

why.plain: Right. DMs notify by default and show up badged and unread. You don't need a mention to get noticed.
why.at: Optimizing for a tab instead of the person. The DM already got their attention.

scenarios.q: In a group DM with your two co-leads, you start a thread and need both to weigh in, though neither has replied yet.

why.plain: Silent miss. In a group DM, only the thread's starter, repliers, and mentioned people get notified, and right now that's just you.
why.at: Right. Starting the thread only subscribes you. To pull both co-leads in, mention them.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you answer the question your coworker asked you in a thread there.

why.plain: Right. 1:1 DM thread, so every reply notifies them by default.
why.at: They asked you the question, in a two-person thread. They're listening.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you're delivering bad news: "@Jo the launch is slipping a week."

why.plain: Right. Bad news lands better as a calm sentence than as a page.
why.at: An @ makes hard news feel like an alarm going off. The DM already got their attention.

scenarios.q: A teammate asks if they should @ you in your DMs "just to be safe."

why.plain: Right. Tell them no. Every DM and every thread reply in a 1:1 DM already notifies you.
why.at: "Just to be safe" is the whole myth in three words. There's no extra safety to buy.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you add an @ because "mobile push notifications only fire on mentions."

why.plain: Right. Slack's notification settings bundle DMs and mentions together ("Direct messages, mentions & keywords"), so a DM already gets the push.
why.at: Mythology. DMs and mentions sit in the same notification bucket.

scenarios.q: In a group DM, you reply to a thread you and Noor have been going back and forth in.

why.plain: Right. Noor's been replying, so Noor is following.
why.at: Redundant. Back-and-forth means Noor's already subscribed.

scenarios.q: In your 1:1 DM, you start a thread under your own message from last week. Jo hasn't replied in it yet, and you want to be sure Jo sees it.

why.plain: Right. In a 1:1 DM, every thread reply notifies both people, whether or not Jo has joined the thread.
why.at: Redundant. Joining a thread only matters in group DMs and channels. In a 1:1 DM, Jo gets every reply anyway.

scenarios.q: In a group DM with Ana and Raj, Ana's thread has only you and Ana in it, and you want Raj to know his PR is the fix.

why.plain: Silent miss. Raj never touched the thread, so in a group DM he won't be notified.
why.at: Right. Group-DM thread, non-participant. The @ is the only thing that reaches Raj.

scenarios.q: In a group DM, you started a thread to ask Mel a question, but Mel hasn't replied in it yet.

why.plain: Silent miss. Starting a thread subscribes you, not Mel, so Mel won't be notified.
why.at: Right. In a group DM, starting a thread doesn't notify the person you're asking. Mention them.

scenarios.q: In a three-person group DM, a thread between you and Sky needs Oz, who hasn't replied, to sign off before you ship.

why.plain: Silent miss. Oz isn't following the thread, so a sign-off request with no @ quietly blocks your ship.
why.at: Right. Oz hasn't started, replied, or been mentioned, and the @ fixes all three at once.

takeaways: In a 1:1 DM, everything notifies by default: top-level messages and every thread reply, even in a thread they haven't joined yet. (Slack: Use threads)
The real exception is a group-DM thread. Someone who didn't start it, reply to it, or get mentioned in it won't hear about replies, so @ them.
An @ won't get through paused notifications. For a real emergency, use the DM's once-a-day override. (Slack: Do Not Disturb)
@ing someone who isn't in the DM doesn't notify them. It works as a profile link, not a ping. (Slack: Use mentions)
